4. Your REPL loop will have to create all filters before starting any of them (think why?)
Poison Pill
An important concept for this assignment is the poison pill. A poison pill is a special message sent to a consumer to signal it to stop waiting for new inputs and end its work. It can take various forms; in this assignment you will use the protected String POISON provided for you in ConcurrentFilter. Filters should send this string to the next filter when they are done processing their input so that the filters in the pipeline know when to stop and do not wait indefinitely for more input from the previous filters.
Background and Foreground Commands
In the second portion of the assignment your task is to add to your REPL support for a simple form of background commands.
A background command does not stop the REPL from accepting further user commands. It runs concurrently with the REPL until completion, allowing the users to start additional background or forward commands. In contrast, a foreground command stops the REPL from accepting further user commands until it has completed processing.
The REPL will allow the user to specify whether a command will run as a foreground command or a background command. In order to start a background command, the user must append an ampersand (&) to the end of the command. For example, “cat large- file.txt &”. Without the ampersand, the command will run as a foreground command.
The user should also be able to list all of the currently running background commands by calling a new command: “repl_jobs” which checks which of the background commands are still running and prints a list of the running commands. To identify the running commands and support command cancellation, repl_jobs will assign a number id to the background commands.
For example:
> cat large-file.txt &
> cat even-larger-file.txt | grep fixme > fixme.txt & > repl_jobs
1. cat large-file.txt &
2. cat even-larger-file.txt | grep fixme > fixme.txt &>
To accurately assess whether a command is still running, you must use the Java Thread object’s isAlive() method.

The user should also be able to kill a specified command by providing the number that “repl_jobs” assigned to it. For example, to kill the second command, user would do:
> kill 2
For a command to be killed, every one of its subcommands needs to stop execution. Stopping a subcommand (a filter) should be done using Java interrupts. Recall that just interrupting a Thread does not stop its execution: the interrupt must be properly handled. Additionally, care must be taken to ensure that the command is killed no matter which stage of its execution the interrupt is made.

**Concurrency Infrastructure**
- Refactor `src/main/java/cs131/pa2/filter/concurrent/ConcurrentFilter.java` to implement `Runnable`, swap `Queue<String>` for `LinkedBlockingQueue<String>`, and drive processing from a new `run()` loop that repeatedly `take`s, skips nulls, forwards processed lines with `put`, and pushes `POISON` downstream on normal completion.
- Extend linking logic in `setPrevFilter`/`setNextFilter` so every connection allocates a shared blocking queue, first filters with no predecessors still receive an initialized output queue, and mismatched filter types throw immediately.
- Add helper hooks (e.g., `setInput`, `setOutput`, `stopProcessing`) to support late queue injection, to guard against `null`, and to let interruptions insert a poison pill for any downstream consumer before exiting.

**Filter Updates**
- Convert source filters (`CatFilter`, `ListFilesFilter`, `PrintWorkingDirectoryFilter`) to override `run()` instead of `process()`: open resources lazily, stream lines via `output.put`, emit `POISON` in `finally`, and honor `Thread.interrupted()` by closing handles promptly.
